anchor_item.prompt: The circuit below shows a 5 V battery in series with 2 5 Ωresistors (R1 and R2).

parts.prompt: On the provided diagram on your answer sheet, clearly draw the direction of conventional current flow in each of the circuit
Calculate the currents through both R1 and R2.
What is the power dissipated by this circuit?
Two 6 Ωresistors (R3 and R4) are added to the initial circuit. Calculate the equivalent resistance of this configuration.
Calculate the current through resistor R1.
Calculate the current through resistor R3.
Calculate the power dissipated by resistor R3.
Calculate the power dissipated by resistor R4.
What is the potential measured at point 1?
What is the potential measured at point 2? Circuit Lab

nodes.label: Initial circuit: 5 V ideal battery in series with two 5 Ω resistors R1 and R2
Conventional current flows from battery positive terminal through external circuit to negative terminal
Ohm’s law and series circuit rules: R_eq_series = R1 + R2, same current through series elements
Power relations: P = VI = I^2 R = V^2 / R
Extended circuit: two 6 Ω resistors R3 and R4 added in a specified configuration (from diagram)
Series/parallel combination rules: R_eq_parallel = 1 / (1/Ra + 1/Rb + ...); series parts add
In a given series branch, current is same through all elements; in parallel branches, voltage across each branch is equal
Voltage division in series: V_element = (R_element / R_total_series) * V_series_total
Reference node / potential: choose one node as 0 V; other node potentials found by summing drops from reference
Part (a): Direction of conventional current indicated correctly on diagram for each branch
Part (b): Numerical value of current through R1 and R2 in initial series circuit
Part (c): Total power dissipated by initial circuit
Part (d): Equivalent resistance of circuit after adding R3 and R4
Part (e): Current through R1 in extended circuit
Part (f): Current through R3 in extended circuit
Part (g): Power dissipated by R3
Part (h): Power dissipated by R4
Part (i): Electric potential at point 1 relative to chosen reference
Part (j): Electric potential at point 2 relative to chosen reference

misconceptions: Using electron flow direction instead of conventional current when drawing arrows
Assuming each series resistor has the full battery voltage across it instead of sharing the voltage
Adding resistances incorrectly for the extended circuit, such as treating parallel branches as series or vice versa
Assuming current is the same in all resistors even when some are in parallel branches
Using total circuit current to compute power in a single resistor without first finding the correct voltage or current for that element
Confusing power formulas and mixing values (e.g., using P = VI with V as battery voltage and I as branch current for a single resistor)
Treating node potentials as absolute rather than relative to a reference, or assuming all points on the positive side of the battery are at the same potential regardless of intervening drops
Neglecting that points connected by ideal wire without intervening elements are at the same potential

question_exemplars.prompt: The circuit below shows a 5 V battery in series with 2 5 Ωresistors (R1 and R2).

parts.prompt: On the provided diagram on your answer sheet, clearly draw the direction of conventional current flow in each of the circuit
Calculate the currents through both R1 and R2.
What is the power dissipated by this circuit?
Two 6 Ωresistors (R3 and R4) are added to the initial circuit. Calculate the equivalent resistance of this configuration.
Calculate the current through resistor R1.
Calculate the current through resistor R3.
Calculate the power dissipated by resistor R3.
Calculate the power dissipated by resistor R4.
What is the potential measured at point 1?
What is the potential measured at point 2? Circuit Lab

nodes.label: Initial circuit: 5 V ideal battery in series with two 5 Ω resistors R1 and R2
Conventional current flows from battery positive terminal through external circuit to negative terminal
Ohm’s law and series circuit rules: R_eq_series = R1 + R2, same current through series elements
Power relations: P = VI = I^2 R = V^2 / R
Extended circuit: two 6 Ω resistors R3 and R4 added in a specified configuration (from diagram)
Series/parallel combination rules: R_eq_parallel = 1 / (1/Ra + 1/Rb + ...); series parts add
In a given series branch, current is same through all elements; in parallel branches, voltage across each branch is equal
Voltage division in series: V_element = (R_element / R_total_series) * V_series_total
Reference node / potential: choose one node as 0 V; other node potentials found by summing drops from reference
Part (a): Direction of conventional current indicated correctly on diagram for each branch
Part (b): Numerical value of current through R1 and R2 in initial series circuit
Part (c): Total power dissipated by initial circuit
Part (d): Equivalent resistance of circuit after adding R3 and R4
Part (e): Current through R1 in extended circuit
Part (f): Current through R3 in extended circuit
Part (g): Power dissipated by R3
Part (h): Power dissipated by R4
Part (i): Electric potential at point 1 relative to chosen reference
Part (j): Electric potential at point 2 relative to chosen reference

misconceptions: Using electron flow direction instead of conventional current when drawing arrows
Assuming each series resistor has the full battery voltage across it instead of sharing the voltage
Adding resistances incorrectly for the extended circuit, such as treating parallel branches as series or vice versa
Assuming current is the same in all resistors even when some are in parallel branches
Using total circuit current to compute power in a single resistor without first finding the correct voltage or current for that element
Confusing power formulas and mixing values (e.g., using P = VI with V as battery voltage and I as branch current for a single resistor)
Treating node potentials as absolute rather than relative to a reference, or assuming all points on the positive side of the battery are at the same potential regardless of intervening drops
Neglecting that points connected by ideal wire without intervening elements are at the same potential
